Photographer Tyler Stalman has once again released his annual iPhone camera review. Below are his thoughts on the iPhone 18 Pro's variable aperture, Photographic Styles, Apple Reference Imagery, and other features.

Stalman takes a deep dive into testing the variable aperture camera of the iPhone 18 Pro

This year's iPhone 18 Pro brings a number of new features, including the 2nm A20 Pro chip, a brand-new vapour chamber, and a smaller Dynamic Island — but the most exciting camera upgrade is undoubtedly the variable aperture system.

Other updates also include Cinematic mode, the addition of Photographic Styles with new texture controls, Apple Reference Imagery, and further refinements to the pro controls in the Camera app.

Today, photographer Tyler Stalman shared his thoughts on the iPhone 18 Pro's new hardware and software camera features. With the review embargo now lifted, reviews from major outlets have been pouring in, including ours at 9to5Mac.

Stalman notes that, while he really liked the cosmic orange colour of last year's iPhone 17 Pro, shooting through glass with it tends to produce reflections. As a result, he recommends that professional photographers consider deep sea blue or black, as these two colours are less likely to introduce unwanted colour casts into photos and videos.

He also mentions at the outset that this review compares the iPhone 18 Pro's camera with the iPhone 15 Pro, and that the review video itself was shot almost entirely on the iPhone 17 Pro.

Speaking of the main camera's headline upgrade — the new variable aperture — Stalman says this feature is "a huge leap in making the iPhone a real camera".

He also points out that the larger f/1.48 aperture lets more light reach the sensor, helping to maintain lower ISOs in low-light conditions and reducing the number of times Night mode kicks in.

This part of the review showcases impressive footage of the aperture blades opening and closing. Stalman notes that one unique aspect of Apple's design is that the aperture blades are placed in front of the main lens group, rather than sitting deep within the optical structure as in traditional camera designs.

Stalman also points out that the 4x zoom on the iPhone 18 Pro (a feature also found on last year's model) is a significant improvement over the 5x zoom on the iPhone 16 Pro, since the 5x focal length can sometimes feel a little too tight.

When it comes to features that may have "gone too far", he briefly mentions the new AI editing tools — such as Clean Up, Extend and Re-Frame — and notes that while these tools are technically impressive and quite realistic, they alter the image so much that the final result loses its original feel.

Discussing the new texture options on the iPhone 18 Pro — Skin, Glow and Film — Stalman demonstrates each option at varying strengths from 0 to 100. His conclusion: Skin subtly reduces skin texture rather than simply blurring skin tones, while Glow produces a diffusion, blooming highlight effect similar to a professional Black Pro-Mist filter.

He is also impressed by the grain and bloom effects of the Film mode, though he wishes Apple would give users finer control over the grain intensity.

The review also covers Apple Reference Imagery, iPhone Cinematic mode (and why Stalman still recommends shooting for a true cinematic look using Apple Log), the new Apple Log 2, and is interspersed with photo and video comparisons between the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 15 Pro.
